```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (identical(Sys.getenv("DRMTMB_CMR_SOURCE"), "true")) {
  devtools::load_all(".", quiet = TRUE)
} else {
  library(drmTMB)
}
```

`drm_cjs()` fits a fixed-effects Cormack–Jolly–Seber model conditional on each
animal's first capture. The survival formula models logit unit-time apparent
survival. Over an interval of length $\Delta$, survival is
$\phi_{\mathrm{unit}}^{\Delta}$; the
detection formula models detection conditional on being alive and surveyed.
This route does not estimate abundance or unseen animals.

Apparent survival combines mortality and permanent emigration; this model
cannot separate them. The contract also excludes all-zero histories, unknown
entry, recruitment, tag loss, temporary emigration, and behavioural trap
dependence. A history whose first capture is its final observation contributes
likelihood one because it has no post-capture information.

## Fit a model

```{r fit}
y <- rbind(
  c(1, 0, 0, 0), c(1, 0, 1, 0), c(1, 1, 0, 0), c(1, 1, 1, 0),
  c(1, 0, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 1, 1), c(1, 1, 0, 1), c(1, 1, 1, 1)
)
d <- cmr_data(y, id = seq_len(nrow(y)), occasions = 1:4, units = "years",
              frequency = c(12, 4, 8, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4))
fit <- drm_cjs(d, phi = ~1, p = ~1)
coef(fit)
```

## Predict and simulate conditionally

Training predictions return only keyed interval and occasion rows that
contribute to the objective.

```{r predict}
pred <- predict(fit)
head(pred$phi[c("id", "interval_start", "phi_unit", "phi_interval")])
head(pred$p)
```

Simulation retains the observed first-capture times, survey masks, and
administrative endpoints. It conditions on the first-capture emission and
keeps death absorbing. Supplying a seed gives reproducible data without
changing the caller's random-number stream.

```{r simulate}
simulated <- simulate(
  fit, nsim = 1L, seed = 20261006
)[[1L]]
refit <- drm_cjs(
  simulated$data, phi = ~1, p = ~1,
  phi_data = simulated$phi_data, p_data = simulated$p_data
)
coef(refit)
```

## Inspect fixed-effect intervals

Wald and profile intervals use the CJS-specific observed likelihood curvature
and constrained CJS refits, respectively. The parametric bootstrap retains
every attempt and its status when the original fit passes admission; an
ineligible original fit can be rejected before an interval result is returned.
Returned results expose a status for each coefficient.
These methods have not passed repeated-sample interval-availability or coverage
qualification. Phase A reports only target-specific single-fit endpoint
capability and status; Phase B will assess repeated-sample availability and
calibration. An available interval does not establish nominal calibration.

```{r intervals}
ci <- confint(fit, method = "wald")
attr(ci, "target_status")
```

## Allow survival to vary among sites

The native R implementation also fits shared site or year effects. This
example uses the same keyed survival-data layout and shared-site formula as the
Julia companion tutorial. The terminal survival constraint resolves the final
survival/detection confounding in this four-occasion example.

```{r shared-site}
n <- 24L
nt <- 4L
ids <- sprintf("animal-%02d", seq_len(n))
sites <- rep(c("north", "south", "east", "marsh", "ridge", "valley"), each = 4L)
y_site <- matrix(0L, n, nt)
y_site[, 1L] <- 1L
for (i in seq_len(n)) for (t in 2:nt)
  y_site[i, t] <- as.integer((i + 2L * t) %% 5L == 0L)
site_data <- cmr_data(y_site, id = ids, occasions = seq_len(nt), units = "years")
phi_data <- data.frame(
  id = rep(ids, each = nt - 1L),
  interval_start = rep(seq_len(nt - 1L), times = n),
  interval_end = rep(2:nt, times = n),
  site = rep(sites, each = nt - 1L)
)
p_data <- data.frame(
  id = rep(ids, each = nt),
  occasion = rep(seq_len(nt), times = n),
  site = rep(sites, each = nt)
)
site_fit <- drm_cjs(
  site_data, phi = ~1 + (1 | site), p = ~1,
  phi_data = phi_data, p_data = p_data,
  terminal_constraint = list(phi = 0.82)
)
coef(site_fit, process = "sd_phi")
site_profile <- confint(
  site_fit, method = "profile", parm = c("phi:(Intercept)", "sd:phi")
)
attr(site_profile, "target_status")
```

## Allow persistent differences among animals

An individual intercept is drawn once for each animal and retained through its
history. This separate R example illustrates a process-specific SD predictor;
the Julia package page uses a compact individual-effects example with different
data and constraints. The shared site-effect example above uses the same
history layout, survival formula, and terminal constraint in both languages.

```{r individual-effects}
set.seed(8102)
n <- 400L
nt <- 5L
ids <- sprintf("bird-%03d", seq_len(n))
z <- rep(c(-1, 0, 1), length.out = n)
phi_sd <- exp(-0.25 + 0.25 * z)
phi_i <- stats::plogis(stats::qlogis(0.82) + stats::rnorm(n, sd = phi_sd))
p_i <- rep(0.58, n)
y_individual <- matrix(0L, n, nt)
y_individual[, 1L] <- 1L
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  alive <- TRUE
  for (t in 2:nt) {
    survival <- if (t == nt) 0.82 else phi_i[[i]]
    alive <- alive && stats::rbinom(1L, 1L, survival) == 1L
    y_individual[i, t] <- if (alive) stats::rbinom(1L, 1L, p_i[[i]]) else 0L
  }
}
individual_data <- cmr_data(y_individual, id = ids, occasions = seq_len(nt),
                            units = "years")
individual_phi_data <- data.frame(
  id = rep(ids, each = nt - 1L),
  interval_start = rep(seq_len(nt - 1L), times = n),
  interval_end = rep(2:nt, times = n),
  z = rep(z, each = nt - 1L)
)
individual_fit <- drm_cjs(
  individual_data, phi = ~1 + (1 | id), p = ~1,
  phi_data = individual_phi_data, sd_phi = ~z,
  terminal_constraint = list(phi = 0.82)
)
coef(individual_fit, process = "sd_phi")
individual_profile <- confint(
  individual_fit, method = "profile",
  parm = c("phi:(Intercept)", "sd_phi:z")
)
attr(individual_profile, "target_status")
c(convergence = individual_fit$convergence,
  gradient_norm = individual_fit$gradient_norm)
pred_individual <- predict(individual_fit, target = "integrated")
head(pred_individual$phi[c("id", "interval_start", "phi_unit", "phi_interval")])
sim_individual <- simulate(individual_fit, nsim = 1L, seed = 8103)[[1L]]
head(sim_individual$data$y)
```

For an integrated interval prediction of length $\Delta$, the target is the
average of conditional survival probabilities raised to that interval length,
$\mathbb{E}_b[s(b)^{\Delta}]$. It is not the marginal unit-time survival
raised to $\Delta$, $\{\mathbb{E}_b[s(b)]\}^{\Delta}$.

The `sd_phi` formula models the log SD of the individual survival effects.
It must use covariates that are known for every contributing interval and
constant within individual. The fitted route can report an SD profile, but
parameter-recovery qualification for this predictor remains open; repeated-sample
interval availability and calibration are deferred to Phase B.
For this fixed demonstration seed, the fitted log-SD coefficients land near the
zero-heterogeneity boundary even though the simulated data use nonzero
heterogeneity. The same likelihood has a nearby interior mode whose minimized
objective is slightly worse. Treat this example as an interface demonstration, not
evidence that the SD predictor was recovered; the programme's paired recovery
design is needed to measure how often this occurs.

The corresponding `sd_p` formula models the log SD of persistent detection
effects. This compact example varies detection heterogeneity by an individual
covariate while keeping survival fixed apart from the terminal constraint.

```{r detection-sd-predictor}
set.seed(8106)
n_detection <- 240L
nt_detection <- 5L
detection_ids <- sprintf("bird-%03d", seq_len(n_detection))
z_detection <- rep(c(-1, 1), length.out = n_detection)
detection_sd <- exp(-0.35 + 0.25 * z_detection)
detection_effect <- stats::rnorm(n_detection, sd = detection_sd)
p_i <- stats::plogis(stats::qlogis(0.58) + detection_effect)
y_detection <- matrix(0L, n_detection, nt_detection)
y_detection[, 1L] <- 1L
for (i in seq_len(n_detection)) {
  alive <- TRUE
  for (t in 2:nt_detection) {
    survival <- if (t == nt_detection) 0.82 else 0.84
    alive <- alive && stats::rbinom(1L, 1L, survival) == 1L
    y_detection[i, t] <- if (alive) stats::rbinom(1L, 1L, p_i[[i]]) else 0L
  }
}
detection_data <- cmr_data(y_detection, id = detection_ids,
                           occasions = seq_len(nt_detection), units = "years")
detection_p_data <- data.frame(
  id = rep(detection_ids, each = nt_detection),
  occasion = rep(seq_len(nt_detection), times = n_detection),
  z = rep(z_detection, each = nt_detection)
)
detection_fit <- drm_cjs(
  detection_data, phi = ~1, p = ~1 + (1 | id), p_data = detection_p_data,
  sd_p = ~z, terminal_constraint = list(phi = 0.82)
)
coef(detection_fit, process = "sd_p")
detection_prediction <- predict(detection_fit, target = "integrated")
head(detection_prediction$p[c("id", "occasion", "p")])
```

The fitted SD coefficients describe the detection log-SD model. This example
checks the public fitting and integrated-prediction route; it does not establish
recovery or interval calibration for detection heterogeneity.

## Correct for first-capture selection

When animals enter a declared alive-and-available reference cohort before they
are first captured, `selection` adds the probability of each observed
first-capture event and divides by its reference-cohort probability. It uses
complete pre-capture survey and covariate histories. The same survival and
detection coefficients govern the pre- and post-capture periods. This
conditional correction describes the declared reference cohort; it does not
estimate unseen animals or abundance.

For individual `i`, the selection-conditioned contribution is the ratio

\[
L_i =
\frac{\int w_i(b) H_i(b) g_{\mathrm{ref}}(b)\,db}
     {\int w_i(b) g_{\mathrm{ref}}(b)\,db},
\]

where `w_i(b)` is the probability of its observed first-capture event from its
declared eligibility occasion, `H_i(b)` is its post-capture CJS history
likelihood, and `g_ref(b)` is the random-effect distribution in the declared
reference cohort. The denominator normalizes by the probability that an
eligible animal is captured, using the same effect distribution as the
numerator.

```{r reference-selection}
set.seed(20261017L)
n_selected <- 144L
nt_selected <- 5L
selected_ids <- sprintf("selected-%03d", seq_len(n_selected))
selected_z <- rep(c(-1, 1), length.out = n_selected)
sigma_phi <- exp(-0.25 + 0.28 * selected_z)
sigma_p <- exp(-0.50 + 0.22 * selected_z)
selected_end <- sample(4:5, n_selected, replace = TRUE)
y_selected <- matrix(0L, n_selected, nt_selected)
first_selected <- integer(n_selected)
for (i in seq_len(n_selected)) {
  repeat {
    phi_effect <- stats::rnorm(1L)
    p_effect <- stats::rnorm(1L)
    history <- integer(nt_selected)
    alive <- TRUE
    for (t in seq_len(selected_end[[i]])) {
      if (t > 1L) {
        alive <- alive && stats::rbinom(
          1L, 1L,
          stats::plogis(stats::qlogis(0.82) + sigma_phi[[i]] * phi_effect)
        ) == 1L
      }
      if (alive) history[[t]] <- stats::rbinom(
        1L, 1L,
        stats::plogis(stats::qlogis(0.56) + sigma_p[[i]] * p_effect)
      )
    }
    captures <- which(history == 1L)
    if (length(captures)) {
      first_selected[[i]] <- captures[[1L]]
      break
    }
  }
  y_selected[i, ] <- history
}
selected_observed <- matrix(TRUE, n_selected, nt_selected)
for (i in seq_len(n_selected)) {
  if (first_selected[[i]] > 2L && y_selected[i, 2L] == 0L)
    selected_observed[i, 2L] <- FALSE
  post_mask <- first_selected[[i]] + 2L
  if (post_mask <= selected_end[[i]] && y_selected[i, post_mask] == 0L)
    selected_observed[i, post_mask] <- FALSE
}
y_selected[!selected_observed] <- NA_integer_
selected_data <- cmr_data(
  y_selected, id = selected_ids, observed = selected_observed,
  occasions = seq_len(nt_selected), end = selected_end, units = "years"
)
selected_phi_data <- data.frame(
  id = rep(selected_ids, each = nt_selected - 1L),
  interval_start = rep(seq_len(nt_selected - 1L), times = n_selected),
  interval_end = rep(2:nt_selected, times = n_selected),
  z = rep(selected_z, each = nt_selected - 1L)
)
selected_p_data <- data.frame(
  id = rep(selected_ids, each = nt_selected),
  occasion = rep(seq_len(nt_selected), times = n_selected),
  z = rep(selected_z, each = nt_selected)
)
selected_fit <- drm_cjs(
  selected_data, phi = ~1 + (1 | id), p = ~1 + (1 | id),
  phi_data = selected_phi_data, p_data = selected_p_data,
  sd_phi = ~1 + z, sd_p = ~1 + z,
  selection = list(eligibility = rep(1L, n_selected),
                   assumption = "alive_available"),
  terminal_constraint = list(phi = 0.82)
)
coef(selected_fit, process = "sd_phi")
coef(selected_fit, process = "sd_p")
pred_selected <- predict(selected_fit, target = "integrated")
selected_profile <- confint(
  selected_fit, method = "profile",
  parm = c("phi:(Intercept)", "sd_phi:(Intercept)", "sd_p:(Intercept)")
)
attr(selected_profile, "target_status")
attr(pred_selected, "prediction")$target
head(pred_selected$p[c("id", "occasion", "p")])
sim_selected <- simulate(selected_fit, nsim = 1L, seed = 8105L)[[1L]]
attr(sim_selected, "simulation")$target
identical(sim_selected$data$first, selected_data$first)
identical(sim_selected$data$observed, selected_data$observed)
identical(sim_selected$data$end, selected_data$end)
```

Prediction and simulation from this fit retain the reference-selection target.
The selection quadrature integrates its numerator and denominator with the same
random-effect law. Integrated predictions average over the selection-weighted
effect distribution given the supplied complete pre-capture history; new data
must provide that history and its survey mask. Correlated random components,
random slopes, structured effects, shared-plus-individual effects, and
shared-effect selection are outside the current contract; unknown entry is
unsupported. Parameter-recovery qualification for this route remains open;
repeated-sample interval studies are deferred to Phase B.

For this fixed seed, the survival and detection SD profile targets are
unavailable, and the survival-intercept profile is partial. The fitted SD
coefficients are extreme in this example, so the output illustrates guarded
status reporting rather than evidence that either SD predictor is identified.

Shared-effect intervals are profile-only; individual-effect coefficient
intervals include profile and parametric-bootstrap methods, while SD formula
coefficients are profile-only. Wald intervals require eligible interior
curvature, and bootstrap can reject a fit before returning attempt records if
it fails admission. Route-specific checks and statuses do not qualify every
route. Phase A reports single-fit endpoint capability and target status only.
Repeated-sample interval availability and coverage/calibration are deferred to
Phase B, so interval availability does not establish nominal calibration. The
`engine = "julia"` bridge remains fixed-effects-only.

## How the R and Julia examples correspond

Read this vignette alongside the Julia pages by scientific task:

| Task | R `drmTMB` section | Julia `DRModels.jl` page |
|---|---|---|
| First-capture conditioning, fixed-effects fit, keyed prediction, conditional simulation, and fixed-effect intervals | “Fit a model”; “Predict and simulate conditionally”; “Inspect fixed-effect intervals” | `cjs.md` |
| Shared site or year variation | “Allow survival to vary among sites” | `cjs-shared-effects.md` |
| Persistent individual effects and process-specific SD predictors | “Allow persistent differences among animals” | `cjs-individual-effects.md` |
| Reference-cohort selection correction | “Correct for first-capture selection” | `cjs-individual-effects.md`, “Predictor-dependent SDs and reference selection” |

The examples implement the same first-capture-conditional estimands and
describe the same exclusions; the table is a reading map, not a claim of
route-wide numerical parity. The shared-site survival example uses the same
histories, formula, and terminal constraint in both packages. Other
demonstrations use package-specific data or API details: R labels its selected
integrated prediction `target = "integrated"`, while Julia uses
`target = :reference_selected`; the R individual-effects example separates
survival and detection SD predictors, while the Julia selection example
demonstrates both together. Interval methods and eligibility rules also differ
by route. Use each package's status output. Phase A does not establish recovery
or repeated-sample interval availability or nominal coverage; those validation
studies are deferred to Phase B.
